The goal might be to make the large square match the small square's pattern at a larger scale. The large square is a 3x3 grid of 5x5 cells, and the small square is a 3x3 grid of 3x3 cells.
Small square's 3x3 cell grid:
- (top-left, top-center, top-right): g, p, g
- (mid-left, center, mid-right): p, g, p
- (bottom-left, bottom-center, bottom-right): g, p, g
Large square's 3x3 cell grid:
- g, W, g
- W, g, W
- g, W, g

How does the token relate? The token is on the track at the top… maybe the token is a "brush" and its position on the track determines which cell of the large square gets painted? The track spans columns 17-42, and the large square spans columns 22-38. If the token is at 23-26, it's above the left column of the large square (24-26)…
Hmm, this is just speculation. Let me try clicking on the cells of the large square and see if they change. For example, click the top-center W cell (50, 30). Or click the center g cell (55, 30).
No, wait. Let me reconsider the role of the token. In many of these generated grid games, the "token" is the player, and the goal is to reach a target. The left square (5x5) might be the "goal" — the player needs to reach it. The notch is blocking the path… unless the notch can be removed by clicking!
Let me try clicking on the notch (21, 19). If the notch disappears, the token can slide all the way to the left square.
